items.title: What is MakeACS?
items.text:
MakeACS is an open-source, modular, low-cost system that makes managing your makerspace, FabLab, or teaching shop easier. The system incorporates machine-level access control, training administration, statistics collection, and shop-management resources like audit logs, maintenance tracking, and inventory control to simplify your workflows. MakeACS can be further augmented via standard API interactions, allowing it to interface with systems like PaperCut, 3DPrinterOS, and student enrollment databases.

MakeACS is 100% open-source, modifying it and hacking it is encouraged! Hardware and firmware is licensed under the CERN-OHL-S 2.0 license, and software is licensed under AGPL-3.0. All source files, documentation, and resources can be found on the MakeACS GitHub, at https://github.com/MakeACS.

MakeACS is developed by the Rochester Institute of Technology's Student Hall for Exploration and Development, with contributions from the open-source community. Learn more about the Student Hall for Exploration and Development at www.rit.edu/shed.

items.title: MakeACS by the Numbers
items.text:
MakeACS currently handles all operations of 7 makerspaces at RIT, with work underway to incorporate MakeACS at other shops at RIT. At least two other universities are also in the process of integrating MakeACS into their shop operations.

As of November 2026, over 200 pieces of MakeACS hardware have been deployed, amassing over 150,000 interactions with makers. The MakeACS server at RIT has administered over 62,000 trainings to the 8,700 registered makers. To date, more than 15,000 unauthorized equipment access attempts have been stopped with MakeACS.

items.title: MakeACS Architecture
items.text:
MakeACS can generally be divided into two parts;

Access Control Hardware is what attaches to equipment to control user access and track utilization.

MakeACS Website is how users and staff interact with the MakeACS system, including the training systems and shop management tools.

items.title: Hardware Overview
items.text:
The MakeACS hardware is what enables the system to control machine-level access, track usage of the shops, and automatically generate maintenance tasks based on usage.

MakeACS hardware is a modular, shared-bus system; multiple individual components can be interconnected to tailor the hardware to the application at hand. Each component is self-contained and in most cases does not require any specialized training or skills to integrate with the equipment.

The MakeACS bus is standardized and easy to integrate into your own device, so you can easily make your own components to suit any need that the already-existing hardware does not.

items.title: The Core
items.text:
The Core is the heart of a MakeACS deployment. It is where the end-user interacts with the system, and is how the deployment communicates with the server.

All Cores are equipped with both a 2.4GHz Wi-Fi radio, and a 100Mbps Ethernet connection, to communicate with the server.

User identification in MakeACS is designed to use already-issued ID cards, such as student IDs or membership cards. Supported cards include:

  • NFC (13.56MHz), ISO/IEC 14443A, MIFARE (Classic, Ultralight, Ultralight C, Plus, DESFire), NTAG
    • Can identify by ISO UID or by decrypting secure application data (such as a student ID number)
  • RFID (125KHz), FSK (HID and HID-compatible, up to 39 bytes), ASK (EM Microelectronic and compatible)
    • Can be configured to use unique card number or facility code + card number for user identification

MakeACS supports two forms of session duration as well;

  • Tap: Works like a traditional card reader, tapping the ID card will start a session of a pre-set length. Tapping again refreshes the countdown.
  • Insert: Requires the card to remain inserted into the MakeACS Core to continue a session duration indefinitely, ensuring constant operator presence.

The Core has a basic RGB LED and buzzer for communicating state, but also has an open-ended connection interface to allow for a display module.

In the event of a network outage, the Core can continue to operate based on an offline list of previously-approved users, for up to 30 days.

The Core can also be used as a sign-in reader to a space. This is useful for collecting statistics of the number of people who enter the space and when, and can also be used to enforce users checking in at the front desk before using equipment for the day.

A MakeACS Core installed on a cold saw.

Tap you ID to activate the paint booth. The display will show you how long you have remaining in your session.

items.title: The Switch
items.text:
The Switch is the part of the access control hardware that actually controls access. There are a number of switches developed for MakeACS, depending on the piece of equipment in use. Multiple switches can also be used together, to form more complex access control setups all from a single card reader.

In most cases, the switch is also where the MakeACS deployment harvests power from, so there is usually no need for an additional power cable or connection. This allows the deployment to be mounted wherever is best for accessability and ergonomics, with no need to worry about additional cables.

items.title: AC Power Switch
items.text:
The AC Power Switch is by far the most popular MakeACS switch. It simply goes inline between the outlet on the wall and your equipment's power cable. There is no need for any invasive in-machine wiring or doing your own AC connections.

The AC Power Switch is rated for highly inductive loads, and can handle a sustained 20A. This makes it ideal for anything from a sewing machine to a bandsaw.

The switch will monitor for any faults such as over-temperature, or blown fuses, and can also be configured to not allow a machine to be activated if it is detected to be in the "on" state.

An AC Power Switch and a Core are the most common deployment.

items.title: USB Hub Switch
items.text:
For a lot of complex equipment, the easiest way to control access to it is by locking down its computer. This strategy works great on laser cutters, water jets, and CNC machines. For this, the USB Hub Switch is a great fit. The switch will activate or de-activate 4 downstream USB ports for keyboards, mice, USB drives, etc.

The USB Hub Switch has a 5th downstream USB port that is connected when the switch is off, which can be used to automatically execute a cleanup script. For instance at RIT, when a user removes their ID card from a laser cutter's computer, it will go through and force-close all windows, make sure the user is logged out of any accounts, etc., before restarting the laser cutter software to give a blank slate to the next user.

items.title: Relay Switch
items.text:
For applications that require more direct integration with equipment, the Relay Switch is the best choice. The relay switch provides galvanically isolated dry contacts, that can be integrated with any arbitrary power or signal to control a piece of equipment. Common examples include interrupting an interlock or e-stop loop, or switching a larger purpose-installed contactor for very large loads like a welding station.

There are 3 variants of the Relay Switch in MakeACS:

  1. The Signal Relay Switch has special gold-plated contacts, allowing it to work with small digital signals, like those from a microcontroller. It has 2 sets of NC and NO contacts, so you can switch multiple things in parallel.

  2. The DIN Relay Switch is rated for 250V at 5A, for integration with larger electrical cabinets. It is usually used to drive a larger contactor.

  3. The DIN Controller is similar to the DIN Relay Switch, but with 5 independent control channels. This allows you more control over how a system is controlled. For example at RIT, this switch is used on the paint booth: the lights, fan, and heater are on 3 separate channels, so anyone can turn on the fan and lights, but only those who are authorized can turn on the burner.

items.title: Other Components
items.text: Beyond simply controlling access, MakeACS supports additional accessories in a deployment, to further augment the capabilities. Here are some examples of these;

items.title: Temperature Monitor
items.text:
The temperature monitor allows an arbitrary temperature probe to be attached to a deployment, that can be used to lock out access if a temperature gets too cold or too hot.

At RIT, this is used to ensure the paint booth is not drawing in too much cold outside air, chilling the entire makerspace.

items.title: Indicator Light
items.text: To help users see equipment availability, this add-on allows the attachment of a standard Andon light tower, which can show deployment state.

items.title: Laser Fume Monitor
items.text: This add-on integrates with the Epilog Laser fume extractor control interface, and will monitor for and report any faults related to the filters or the air assist supply line. If either is found to be malfunctioning, the equipment is locked out automatically.

items.title: Hobbs Timer
items.text: While MakeACS automatically tracks usage time based on the total time on, this add-on allows for a specific signal to be used for hours tracking. This is useful on something like a CNC, where maintenance tasks should be based on spindle run-time, versus machine on-time.

items.title: Buddy System Enforcer
items.text:
This add-on lets two Cores control one deployment, in one of three modes. This allows hardware-enforcement of the buddy policy on high-risk equipment, or more complex user authorization setups.

  • AND Mode: Both Cores need an approved user present to activate the equipment. This ensures 2 trained users are present at all times.

  • OR Mode: Either Core needs an approved user to activate the equipment. This allows trained users to hand off equipment without disrupting its operation.

  • AND-OR Mode: Both Cores need an approved user to activate, but then either one can keep it online. This is useful on equipment where you want staff to check over things before the user starts running, but once it is approved they can work on their own.

items.title: Blast Gate Controller
items.text: This add-on enables MakeACS to open blast gates based on what equipment is in use. This ensures maximum suction to the equipment in use, and prevents excessive wear on the vacuum system when nothing is un use. It is designed for use with iVac automated blast gates, but can work with any generic 12v blast gate system.

items.title: Deployment Examples
items.text: Below are some examples of how MakeACS is deployed at RIT.

items.title: AC Power Switch
items.text:
The AC Power Switch is by far the most common switch. RIT uses it on the following machines;

  • Bernina 475, 590, E16, L460, Q20
  • Weller soldering iron
  • Metcal soldering heat gun
  • Roland RS-24 Vinyl Cutter
  • Bantam CNC mill
  • Laguna bandsaw, belt sander, drum sander, jointer
  • Powermatic drill press
  • Jet bandsaw, edge sander
  • Generic panel saw
  • Generic rotary grinding/sanding tool

items.title: Haas CNC Machines
items.text:
All Haas CNC machines produced after 2014 ship with an NGC (Next Generation Controller). This controller has a dedicated auxiliary E-stop plug, intended for connecting a robot or other automation system. This connection can instead be connected to a Relay Switch.

Power for the system can come from the spare 110V outlets found inside most Haas electrical cabinets.

Source: HaasCNC.com

items.title: Fablight Laser Cutter
items.text:
The Fablight Laser Cutter has an spare interlock loop in an access panel on the left side of the machine, intended for use with a tube-extension add-on. A Relay Switch interrupting this connection is read as a door-open fault, and the machine will not move or fire the laser until a card is present.

Power for the system can come from open USB ports inside the electrical cabinet.

items.title: ProtoTrak Mill
items.text:
KMX-controller ProtoTrak machines have an auxiliary E-stop plug in the back of the machine, labeled "EURO E-STOP". By default, it ships with a jumper head on it that connects pins 1-6, 2-4, 3-5, and 7-8-9. Interrupting the 2-4 connection with a Relay Switch puts the controller in an emergency lockout state, making the machine inoperable but without losing any of the parameters saved in the controller.

On KMX machines with a power knee, RIT also installs an AC Power Switch, so that the knee's power is cut when a card is not present.

items.title: Epilog Laser Cutter
items.text:
Epilog lasers can take up to a minute to start up, so cutting their power is not ideal. Instead, at RIT access control restricts use of the computer used to send jobs to the laser, by interrupting their keyboard, mouse, and exposed USB ports with a USB Hub Switch.

This has the added benefit of running an automatic cleanup script when a user is done with the computer, ensuring all their work is closed and all accounts are logged out, so every user has a clean-slate experience.

items.title: OMAX Waterjet
items.text: OMAX waterjets are intended to be constantly connected to an operator computer. By interrupting the computer's keyboard and mouse with a USB Hub Switch, the user cannot activate the pump or start a cut. The benefit of this is that it does not interfere with any critical interfaces, such as the E-stop or feed hold buttons, meaning they are always readily available in the event of an emergency.

items.title: Generic Lab Computers
items.text: For lab computers with software or licenses that do not play well with individual user accounts, a USB Hub Switch controlling access to a computer can help keep a record of users, and reset the computer to a known state after each use, with the help of software like Deep Freeze.

items.title: Hardware API
items.text: MakeACS hardware communicates with the MakeACS server via a standardized MQTT API. This API structure can be adopted by other systems, to allow MakeACS hardware to be used with your own system. See the MakeACS Hardware Standards for more information.

items.title: 3. Server Features
items.text:
The server (aka the website) is how all makers and staff interact with MakeACS, as well as the central source of information for the MakeACS hardware.

The website is designed to require minimal resources to host, with hosting from most providers working out to under $30 per month. It can also easily be deployed in a docker container for hosting in on-campus IT infrastructure, to both save costs and comply with institutional data handling policies.

The website implements Shibboleth SAML Single Sign On, to easily integrate into existing systems. Local accounts are possible for institutions that do not have SSO, or for special non-SSO cases, like organization accounts.

The website's appearance is fully customizable without any coding, and supports multiple appearance skins that users can select from (such as a dark or light mode, seasonal themes, etc.)

items.title: Public Information
items.text:
The website hosts a public-facing website for the shops, with useful information for the general public;

  • Facility hours, with support for special-case hours and differing hours for different rooms.
  • Announcements with an integrated call-to-action link.
  • Facility information such as locations, links to maps, etc.
  • General machine information.
  • Real-time equipment availability, to see if what you are looking to use is free.
  • A publicly-available REST API for getting the hours, announcements, etc. for integration into other systems and websites.
  • Upcoming events, pulled via API from systems like Eventbrite

Additionally, the website generates and serves pages for the hours, announcements, and events that can be constantly displayed on screens around the facility, that will automatically update as changes are made to the website, and handle anti-burn in image shifting.

Check it out yourself; make.rit.edu/app/display/hours/36

Upcoming Events, Hours, and Announcements Displays

items.title: Maker (User) Features
items.text: Once a maker signs in, they can access more features of the website;

items.title: SSO Information Sync
items.text:
TOn log-in the system can get a user's preferred name, preferred pronouns, and profile picture. This information can then be readily accessed by staff, to ensure they are properly addressing users as they work in the shop. If a user's preferred pronouns are not yet updated at the SSO-level, they can be manually changed within their user preferences.

The system can also be configured to restrict a user account based on SSO information. For instance, at RIT alumni maintain their normal SSO account, but are no longer allowed to use the makerspaces. So, when an alumni logs into the website, their account is flagged and put into an archived state, where they can no longer use equipment.

Analytical data can also be collected via SSO and plotted against other data gathered about shop operation, such as correlating equipment usage trends to home college, or makerspace utilization vs. expected graduation year.

User info, visible to staff, pulled from SSO

items.title: Trainings
items.text:
One of the main features used by makers on the website is the training system. Online trainings are a great way to reinforce general safety and usage concepts before users step foot in the shop. Trainings consist of multiple-choice questions supporting either single-answer or multiple-answer results. The training system also supports embedding images, PDFs, videos, and markdown-formatted text directly inside the training.

An example of an embedded video training

When a user completes a training, they can be given customized affirmations and/or hints to either reinforce concepts, or give them a nudge towards the correct answer.

Shop administrators can set pass and refresh policies for trainings. For instance, RIT requires an 80% or higher to have considered "passing" a training, and makes any training related to safety expire annually, whereas technical trainings last forever.

To prevent brute-forcing, the website automatically locks out a user for 24 hours if they attempt and fail a training 3 times in a day. This is logged for auditing, and can be overridden by staff if needed.

Training content can be reciprocal across any equipment within the same MakeACS server. For example, at RIT there is a generic "How to use the MakeACS card reader" training that is required before using any equipment. Once the user completes it in the machine shop, it is reciprocally granted in the sewing shop, for example.

Training content can be associated with equipment, rooms, or the entire makerspace to ensure consistent application of policies.

As a training approaches expiration, makers are automatically sent reminder emails, with a call to action on what trainings to complete to continue having access to which equipment(s).

I'll lose access to the 3D printers if I don't re-do my training!

To help inform users about training requirements, every piece of equipment on the website has a checklist and a progress bar. The website also generates mobile-friendly training checklists, intended for use with a QR code on the machine.

"Makerspace Requirements" apply to all equipment everywhere.

items.title: Reservations
items.text:
While the default behavior of equipment in MakeACS is first-come, first-serve, the system also implements a reservation calendar. Equipment can be configured to have a self-schedule calendar where anyone can put a reservation down, or staff-schedule, where users muse work with staff to schedule an appointment. Appointment scheduling can optionally be blocked behind the same training access checks that machine access would, so users cannot reserve equipment they cannot use.

When a reservation is submitted, staff with authority to approve it can be notified by email or Slack message.

The self-serve reservation calendar

items.title: Staff Features
items.text: System administrators can designate two tiers of staff within MakeACS; staff, and managers. These roles can be assigned on a per-space basis, so staff only have elevated permissions in areas they work in. With a staff account, more features become available;

items.title: Staff Sign-Off
items.text:
Trainings can be just one part of granting access to equipment; the system can be configured to also (or instead of trainings) require an in-person staff sign-off on a per-machine basis. These trainings can have a configurable expiration policy, and can be set to either be permitted by any staff, or a select list of authorized trainers.

Staff Sign-Offs are visible to other staff as a way of verifying training completion, or if needed a way to revoke equipment access, and a record is kept of which staff completed a user's training.

items.title: Audit Logs
items.text:
All activities in the facility is tracked in a centralized audit log/history. Log information can be sorted and searched by keywords, category, or date range. System administrators can set certain information to not be visible to all staff, such as training grades.

The audit log embeds useful click-through links. For example, the audit log of "Jim Heaney has signed into the Atrium Makerspace" has a click-through to Jim Heaney's user account, so staff can quickly access information on them.

Audit log content can also be fed into systems like Grafana to develop graphical data representations, identify trends, or have real-time heads-up information about the shop. For example, the visualization below allows tracking of sign-ins to a space per hour, to identify what times need additional staffing.

items.title: Maintenance Logs
items.text:
To aid in tracking equipment issues, a maintenance logging system is available to all staff. Staff can open reports with issues they find, and attach images to assist in future diagnostics. Which staff claim/close a ticket, how long the ticket took to close, and how often tickets of a set severity level are registered against a piece of equipment are all logged for statistical analysis.

When a maintenance ticket is generated, it can be used to trigger an automatic email or Slack message, to keep maintenance staff informed about ongoing issues.

In addition to reported issues, the MakeACS server can automatically generate tickets, based on 2 different criteria;

  • Time-based tickets are opened a set interval after their last iteration were closed. An example is a weekly reminder to check the eye wash stations.

  • Usage-based tickets are opened after a set amount of on-time from the MakeACS hardware. An example is a ticket to change the oil on the waterjet every 50 hours.

Maintenance logs that are marked with a high severity can be configured to automatically lock out equipment and deny all access attempts.

"SERVER" tickets are for scheduled/regular maintenance

items.title: Equipment State
items.text:
Staff have the ability to see the equipment's current state, and remotely change the equipment's state via the website. This allows them to lock equipment on during workshops or trainings, or lock it off when the equipment should not be used. Staff are only able to lock equipment on that they themselves are trained on, to prevent system bypasses. If staff forget to return equipment from the locked-on to regular mode, systems re-lock automatically at 4am every morning. Locked out equipment will maintain its state, even through a loss-of-power.

Staff can see the current equipment state, and either the current user or what staff commanded it into that state via the website.

items.title: Inventory Control
items.text:
The MakeACS server supports a full inventory management system, which can be modified by staff actions via the website, or automatically via API. Staff can add or remove inventory via the normal MakeACS website, or via special mobile-optimized pages that are intended to be on QR codes directly attached to the inventory.

Managers can set categories, price points, and restock policies for all inventory. When inventory goes below a set threshold, the system can automatically send a Slack or email notification to trigger a re-order.

Inventory items can have images or notes attached to them, to help staff identify them or to have re-order information on hand in one centralized location.

items.title: Tool Loan Tracking
items.text:
For high-value or high-risk equipment, the website has a tool loan tracking system. Users can check out equipment with a staff member, and return it when complete. If a user forgets to return equipment for more than 24 hours, a flag is put up to follow up with the user.

Upon loaning or returning equipment, staff can be presented with images and/or formatted text, to verify they are giving the correct item and everything is as it should be. Staff can note damage or issues upon return for investigation.

The condition and current loan status of all equipment can be seen from a centralized interface, and is also available for statistical analysis via the audit log.

For further analytics collection specifically surrounding the website, you can enter a custom Google Analytics ID to gain usage information, such as common pages, traffic sources, and bounce rates.

items.title: User Restrictions
items.text:
In the event that staff find a user acting in an improper or dangerous way in the makerspace, they have the ability to place a restriction on their account. This will flag their account for review by a manager, and stop them from using any equipment in the makerspace until it is resolved.

Managers have the ability to place a hold on a user's account, which stops them from using all equipment under MakeACS, notifies staff if they attempt to sign in to a makerspace, and locks down their view of the website. Even when removed, a permanent record of a hold is left on the user's account.

Staff and managers can also see and edit notes on a user's account, to help log information for other staff.

items.title: Organizations & Finances
items.text:
Managers have the ability to credit user accounts with a virtual currency - Construct Credits - that can be used to purchase items from inventory, or as part of automated payment integrations with systems like 3DPrinterOS, in addition to PaperCut.

In addition to being able to issue such credits to individual users, managers can create organization accounts and issue credits to them. This allows research labs, student teams, and more to operate under one financial umbrella, rather than having to designate a single point-of-contact.
